title: Recording set-up; birth and premature infancy; old log homesteads
description: Dale Anderson opens the interview with Minnie Badgett at St. Mary's, Idaho, on June 20, 1975. Minnie tells of being born prematurely at home in 1901 near the Santa crossroads with a nurse's help. She then describes the old log homesteads around the country, their hewn construction, dirt foundations, shake roofs and gradual decay.

title: Parents and siblings; husband and children
description: Minnie gives biographical details about her mother Frances O'Nelia Rothrock and father Frederick Scott, a logger and small farmer, and names her five brothers and five sisters with their married names. She then describes her husband Ralph Badgett, their 1921 marriage in Walla Walla, and their children Vernon, Virgil and Velma, their births and later occupations.

title: Schooling; jobs; needlework; clubs
description: Minnie describes her eighth-grade education and abbreviated high school years working for board in St. Mary's, her jobs waiting tables in logging camps and doing housework, and her crocheting and embroidery learned from her mother. She lists her memberships in the Grange, Eagles, VFW ladies' clubs and a social 'Know Nothing Club' where women lunch and do needlework.

title: Early Emida; naming the town; neighborly help; childhood work and play
description: Minnie recounts early settlement around Emida, including how the town's name was formed from the initials of the East, Miller and Dawson families when a post office was sought. She describes how neighbors shared butchered beef, garden produce, clothing and sewing with poorer families, and recalls her childhood work, ball games, fishing, horseback riding and house parties.

title: Fishing and hunting changes; siblings' work; courtship and marriage
description: Minnie contrasts the free fishing and hunting of her youth with modern game laws and notes the later appearance of elk. She says her brothers all logged and her sisters became housewives, then recounts meeting Ralph through family connections, courting at dances and church, and marrying at nineteen, with her thoughts on marriage ages and divorce.

title: Children, doctor books; grandchildren's work; difficult daughter-in-law
description: Minnie discusses raising children with the help of home doctor books and distant doctors in St. Mary's and Tekoa. She details her grandchildren, including Judy, a technician in Texas, Kelvin and Dale working at the pole company, and Barry in the Navy in Japan, and frankly describes her strained relations with Jake's wife.

title: Sewing; grandson's death; Depression and wartime
description: Minnie tells of teaching her daughter to sew, of a grandson who died of leukemia at eight, and of cancer deaths in Ralph's family. She describes surviving the Depression through gardening, dairying, threshing and hay baling, and how dealing honestly with mortgage companies saved their farm when neighbors lost theirs, then says World War II was harder, with Jake serving overseas.

title: Family life today; cars for grandchildren; friendship with Shannon
description: Minnie describes ordinary days with children and sewing, then her practice of buying cars for grandchildren, including one she let Barry's girlfriend Shannon use for nursing training in Spokane. She warmly recounts shared dinners with Shannon and Shannon's mother, and says the family does not gather often.

title: Children's jobs; recreation; timber land
description: Minnie describes her teenagers working at local shops, her own crocheting and potlucks, and how the family bought 1,400 acres of timber from the Goldie Lumber Company for two to nine dollars an acre.

title: Fires; land sale; farm management
description: She recounts three suspicious fires in the timber, the decision to sell the acreage to avoid trouble, and selling the farm in 1966 when she could get Social Security.

title: Farm maintenance; selling; St. Maries
description: The discussion turns to the difficulty of maintaining fences and meadow ground, why she moved to St. Maries, and buying a small house for son Jake and his wife.

title: Moving to town; wagon wreck
description: Minnie explains her move to St. Maries after her husband's death and tells the story of a freight wagon runaway that left a wagon tongue embedded in a tree.

title: Books; travel; Los Angeles
description: She discusses history books she owns, visitors from Iowa and North Carolina, trips to visit family, and her preference for small-town life over Los Angeles.

title: Food; soap; household work
description: The conversation covers gardening, cellar storage, canning, drying, making soap, and the constant daily labor of washing, ironing, and cooking in the past.

title: Modern conveniences; media; decisions
description: Minnie reflects on her first washing machine, sewing machines, television shows, magazine subscriptions, and her husband's role in making farm decisions.

title: Widowhood; advice
description: She talks about adjustments to living alone, eating habits, companionship with other ladies, and general advice about life.

title: Women's roles; working mothers
description: Minnie offers her views on professional women, social classes, and the importance of mothers staying home with young children rather than working.

title: Winter games; taffy pulls
description: She concludes with memories of childhood sleigh riding, skating, fox and geese games, and taffy pull parties.
